answer:
`keep_firing_for` is an optional clause that keeps an alert firing for a set duration after its firing condition was last met.[1]
You can use it to prevent flapping alerts and false resolutions.[1]
Without `keep_firing_for`, an alerting rule deactivates on the first evaluation where the condition is not met, provided any `for` duration has been satisfied.[1]
In the example rule, it is set with `keep_firing_for: 5m` next to `for: 10m`.[1]

answer:
`.spec.progressDeadlineSeconds` is an optional field that sets how many seconds to wait for a Deployment to progress before the system reports that it has failed progressing.[1]
It defaults to 600.[1]
If you set it, it must be greater than `.spec.minReadySeconds`.[1]
When the deadline is exceeded, the Deployment controller adds a condition to `.status.conditions` with `type: Progressing`, `status: "False"` and `reason: ProgressDeadlineExceeded`.[2]
The Deployment controller will keep retrying the Deployment.[1]
Besides reporting this condition, Kubernetes takes no action on a stalled Deployment, but higher-level orchestrators can use the condition, for example to roll back.[2]
You can set it with `kubectl patch`, for example `kubectl patch deployment/nginx-deployment -p '{"spec":{"progressDeadlineSeconds":600}}'`.[2]
The deadline stops applying once the rollout completes.[2]
The deadline is also not checked while a rollout is paused.[2]

answer:
Create a headless Service: set `.spec.clusterIP` to `"None"` explicitly.[1]
Leave `.spec.type` as ClusterIP, which is also the default for `type`.[1]
`None` is a special value, so leaving the field unset does not do the same thing.[1]
With this setup the Service gets no cluster IP, kube-proxy does not handle it, and the platform does no load balancing or proxying.[1]
Instead of a virtual IP, the cluster's DNS service publishes each pod's IP, so clients connect to pods directly.[1]

You can use `configMapKeyRef` under `env[].valueFrom` to put a ConfigMap value into a Pod's environment variables.[1]
Use this `env.valueFrom` syntax to pick individual keys from a ConfigMap, and the variable name doesn't have to match the key.[2]

answer:
A Pod stuck in the `Terminating` state means a deletion was issued, but the control plane cannot delete the Pod object.[1]
This usually happens when the Pod has a finalizer and an admission webhook in the cluster stops the control plane from removing that finalizer.[1]
To confirm this, check whether your cluster has a `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration` or `MutatingWebhookConfiguration` that targets `UPDATE` operations for `pods` resources.[1]
The passage cuts off before the fix steps for third-party webhooks and for your own webhooks, so it doesn't cover how to resolve the problem.

answer:
Add `for: 10m` to the alerting rule.[1]
The optional `for` clause makes Prometheus wait for a set duration between first seeing a new expression output vector element and counting the alert as firing for it.[1]
With `for: 10m`, Prometheus checks on every evaluation for 10 minutes that the alert is still active, and only then fires it.[1]
While it waits, the alert is in the pending state.[1]
If you leave out `for`, the alert becomes active on the first evaluation.[1]

answer:
Before installing Argo CD, you need the `kubectl` command-line tool installed.[2]
You also need a kubeconfig file, which by default is at `~/.kube/config`.[2]
Your cluster must have CoreDNS, which you can enable on microk8s with `microk8s enable dns && microk8s stop && microk8s start`.[2]
If you install into a namespace other than `argocd`, first update the namespace reference in the `ClusterRoleBinding` resources.[1]

answer:
No, a Deployment with `.spec.revisionHistoryLimit` set to 0 cannot be rolled back.[1]
Setting the field to zero removes every old ReplicaSet that has 0 replicas, so you can't undo a new rollout.[2]
This happens because each revision's configuration is stored in its ReplicaSet, so deleting that ReplicaSet removes the ability to roll back to that revision.[2]
The cleanup only starts after the Deployment reaches a complete state.[1]
To be able to use `kubectl rollout undo` again, set `.spec.revisionHistoryLimit` above 0; the default keeps 10 old ReplicaSets.[2]

answer:
No, Kubernetes does not roll the Deployment back; it only reports a status condition with `reason: ProgressDeadlineExceeded`.[3]
The Deployment controller also keeps retrying the Deployment.[1]
Rolling back is left to higher-level orchestrators, or you can do it yourself.[3]
To roll back to the previous revision, run `kubectl rollout undo deployment/nginx-deployment`.[2]
To roll back to a specific revision, add `--to-revision`, for example `kubectl rollout undo deployment/nginx-deployment --to-revision=2`.[2]
To check that the rollback worked, run `kubectl get deployment nginx-deployment`.[2]

answer:
Run `argocd admin initial-password -n argocd` to get the first admin password.[2]
The password is auto-generated and stored in clear text in the `password` field of the `argocd-initial-admin-secret` secret.[2]
To reach the API server without exposing the service, run `kubectl port-forward svc/argocd-server -n argocd 8080:443`.[1]
You can then open it at https://localhost:8080.[1]
Log in with the username `admin` and that password using `argocd login <ARGOCD_SERVER>`.[2]
You can also have the CLI port-forward for you: add `--port-forward-namespace argocd` to every command, or run `export ARGOCD_OPTS='--port-forward-namespace argocd'`.[2]
After that, change the password with `argocd account update-password` and delete `argocd-initial-admin-secret`.[2]

Pods that mount the ConfigMap as files pick up the change without a restart, but pods that read it as environment variables do not.[2]
The kubelet checks on every periodic sync whether the mounted ConfigMap is fresh, but it reads the value from its local cache.[2]
So the update can take as long as the kubelet sync period plus the cache propagation delay to appear.[2]
You can set the cache type with the `configMapAndSecretChangeDetectionStrategy` field in the KubeletConfiguration struct.[2]
Environment variables only change after a pod restart.[2]
If the ConfigMap is immutable (`immutable: true`), you cannot change its `data` or `binaryData` at all, so you have to delete it and recreate it.[1]
Existing pods keep a mount point to the deleted ConfigMap, so the documentation recommends recreating those pods too.[1]

answer:
The passages cover two kinds of timeout in Argo CD, and both are set in `argocd-cm`.
**Application reconciliation timeout**
Set `timeout.reconciliation` to control how long Argo CD waits before checking the repository for a new manifests version.
The example value is `timeout.reconciliation: 120s`, and setting it to 0 turns off reconciliation by timeout.[1]
You can spread refreshes out by also setting `timeout.reconciliation.jitter`, which defaults to 1 minute.[1]
After you change this setting, you have to restart the `argocd-repo-server` deployment and the `argocd-application-controller` statefulset yourself.
**Extension backend timeouts**
Under `extension.config`, `connectionTimeout` sets how long a dial to the extension server waits to connect, and the default is 2 seconds.
`idleConnectionTimeout` sets how long an idle keep-alive connection stays open before it closes, and the default is 60 seconds.
The passages don't cover timeouts in Kubernetes or Prometheus.

answer:
The answer depends on where you want the labels; the passages cover four cases.
Prometheus alert labels go under `labels:` in an alerting rule, and their values can be templated with variables such as `$labels` and `$value`.[1]
For example, the `InstanceDown` rule adds `severity: page`.[1]
To add Application labels to the Kubernetes events Argo CD generates, list the `metadata.labels` keys in `resource.includeEventLabelKeys`.[2]
The example value is `resource.includeEventLabelKeys: team,env*`, and wildcards are supported.[2]
To show custom labels in the Argo CD UI, set `resource.customLabels` as a comma-separated string and restart the Application Controller.[4]
For a Kubernetes Deployment, `.spec.template.metadata.labels` must be set explicitly and must match `.spec.selector`.[3]
The passages do not explain how to add labels to an arbitrary Kubernetes object, for example with a `kubectl` command.

answer:
Change the password with `argocd account update-password` after logging in as `admin`.[1]
1. Get the initial `admin` password with `argocd admin initial-password -n argocd`.[1]
2. Log in with the username `admin` and that password using `argocd login <ARGOCD_SERVER>`.[1]
3. Run `argocd account update-password`.[1]
4. Then delete the `argocd-initial-admin-secret` from the Argo CD namespace.[1]
If the CLI can't reach the API server directly, add `--port-forward-namespace argocd` to every command or set it in `ARGOCD_OPTS`.[1]
The new password must match the regex in `passwordPattern` in `argocd-cm`.[2]

answer:
Kubernetes does not roll back a failed Deployment by itself; it only reports a status condition with `reason: ProgressDeadlineExceeded`.[1]
Higher-level orchestrators can use that condition to act, for example by rolling the Deployment back to its previous version.[1]
How long it waits before reporting a stalled rollout is set by `.spec.progressDeadlineSeconds`.[1]
For example, setting `progressDeadlineSeconds` to `600` makes the controller report a stalled rollout after 10 minutes.[1]
When the deadline passes, the controller adds a condition to `.status.conditions` with `type: Progressing`, `status: "False"` and `reason: ProgressDeadlineExceeded`.[1]

answer:
A headless Service is a Service that has no single Service IP and does no load-balancing.[1]
To define one, set `.spec.type` to `ClusterIP` and also set `.spec.clusterIP` to `None`.[1]
It does not get a cluster IP, and kube-proxy does not handle it.[1]
Clients connect directly to Pods, whose IP addresses are reported through the cluster's DNS records.[1]
If the Service defines selectors, DNS returns A or AAAA records that point directly to the Pods behind the Service.[2]
If it has no selectors, no EndpointSlice objects are created, and the `port` must match the `targetPort`.[3]

5. `.spec.strategy.rollingUpdate.maxSurge` is optional and sets the maximum number of Pods that can be created over the desired number, as an absolute number or a percentage that defaults to 25%.[2]
`maxUnavailable` and `maxSurge` cannot both be 0.[2]

answer:
Pause the Deployment before you make your updates, then resume it when you're ready to apply them, so several fixes don't each trigger a rollout.[1]
1. Pause it with `kubectl rollout pause deployment/nginx-deployment`.[1]
2. Make your changes, for example `kubectl set image deployment/nginx-deployment nginx=nginx:1.16.1`.[1]
3. You can make as many updates as you want, for example `kubectl set resources deployment/nginx-deployment -c=nginx --limits=cpu=200m,memory=512Mi`.[1]
4. Check with `kubectl rollout history deployment/nginx-deployment` that no new rollout has started.[1]
5. Resume the Deployment to start a new rollout with all your fixes.[3]
You can also pause through the optional boolean field `.spec.paused`.[2]
While a Deployment is paused, changes to its PodTemplateSpec don't trigger new rollouts.[2]
The passages don't give the exact resume command, and they don't cover Argo Rollouts canary pauses at all.

answer:
Use controller RBAC with `resource.respectRBAC`, or a label selector with `resource.selectors`; the passages don't say how to set up `resource.exclusions`, the direct way to drop whole kinds.
**Option 1: deny the kinds through controller RBAC**
You can keep the Argo CD controller from discovering or syncing specific resources with controller RBAC alone, without setting up resource exclusions by hand.[1]
To turn this on, set the `resource.respectRBAC` key in the `argocd-cm` ConfigMap, and the controller will stop watching resources it isn't allowed to list or access.[1]
To keep API server calls as low as possible, use `normal`, which skips the extra `SelfSubjectAccessReview` call.[1]
`strict` is more accurate but sends more calls to the kube api-server.[1]
**Option 2: filter objects with `resource.selectors`**
`resource.selectors` limits which objects of a group/kind Argo CD watches, and the objects it filters out never reach Argo CD.[2]
Each rule matches on `apiGroups`, `kinds` and `clusters`, and applies a `selector` written in string form, such as `!tier`.[2]
**What the passages leave out**
The passages say that `resource.inclusions` and `resource.exclusions` work at the group/kind level, but they don't show how to configure them.[2]
They also don't say how much memory any of these options saves.

answer:
Add a `profile` field to the `awsAuthConfig` in the cluster Secret's `config`, set to the path of the AWS credentials file. Argo CD release 2.10 added this option[1]
In the example, `awsAuthConfig` sets `clusterName`, `roleARN` and `profile`[1]
The Secret needs the label `argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type: cluster`[1]
Argo CD then reads that file and uses the credentials in it to authenticate to AWS[1]
You must mount the profile file in both `argocd-server` and `argocd-application-controller`[1]
You still need the IAM steps and the `aws-auth` config map so the principal can access the cluster[2]
The passages stop before showing the Helm values for mounting the profile file.

answer:
Create a Kustomize-based Argo CD Application that uses the base Argo CD manifests from https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd and layers your changes on top.[1]
Argo CD can manage itself because all of its settings are Kubernetes manifests.[1]
1. In `kustomization.yaml`, list `github.com/argoproj/argo-cd//manifests/cluster-install?ref=stable` under `resources`, along with your own resources such as cluster and repository secrets.
2. Put ConfigMap changes under `patches`, for example `- path: overlays/argo-cd-cm.yaml`.
3. Enable the `ServerSideApply=true` sync option, because it is required when Argo CD manages itself.[2]
4. The example Application is named `argocd`, uses `path: manifests/cluster-install` with `targetRevision: stable`, and sets `syncPolicy.automated` with `prune: true` and `selfHeal: true`, plus `syncOptions: - ServerSideApply=true`.
5. Make customizations through Kustomize patches in your configuration repository, not by editing the live resources by hand.[2]
Server-side apply is needed because some Argo CD CRDs, such as ApplicationSet, are larger than the 262KB annotation size limit of client-side `kubectl apply`.[3]
A live example runs at https://cd.apps.argoproj.io, and its configuration is stored in argoproj/argoproj-deployments.

answer:
Generate the SBOM in a standardized format such as SPDX, Cyclone DX or SWID.[1]
Standard formats like CycloneDX and SPDX let different tools and platforms communicate consistently.[2]
Create the SBOM at build time from the source code, and link it to the SBOMs of the libraries and tools you import.[1]
Build tools are the best producers of accurate, attested SBOMs, because the build is the only point where source code, dependencies and the produced software all come together.
Generating SBOMs after the build by scanning package manager indexes can be error-prone.[2]
Post-build SBOM generators can still be used to check that the build-time SBOM is accurate.[1]
The CI/CD system should sign both the application and the container images, and those signatures should be reproduced in the SBOM.[1]

answer:
The CNCF whitepaper lists these practices for protecting the Git repository used in GitOps, based on least privilege and separation of duties.[1]
1. Restrict access to the repository and its branches.[1]
2. Never store unencrypted credentials or secrets in the repository, and block sensitive data from being pushed to Git.[1]
3. Require GPG signed commits so there is a strong identity behind each change, which gives accountability and traceability.[1]
4. Require linear history and keep the commit history by disallowing force pushes.[1]
5. Enforce a branching policy, especially protecting the main branch and requiring code review before merging.[1]
6. Monitor for vulnerabilities and keep Git and GitOps tools up to date.[1]
7. Rotate SSH keys and Personal Access Tokens, and block unauthorized access to Git repositories.[1]
8. Use a dedicated non-user technical account for access, with credentials that are rotated often and short-lived.[2]
9. Limit which users can raise permissions to remove security features, because those users could delete audit trails and silence alerts to cover their tracks.[2]
These controls matter because an attacker who compromises the GitOps process may open infrastructure backdoors or introduce harmful software to production.[1]

With CaaS, users still orchestrate and manage the containers, applications and clusters themselves, using a container-based virtualization platform together with an API or a web portal management interface.[1]
In CaaS, containers are the basic resource the user works with.[1]
With FaaS, the cloud service provider handles the physical hardware, the virtual machine operating system and the web server software automatically.[1]
This means FaaS users only need to focus on individual functions in their microservices code, and they pay only for the resources they use.[1]

answer:
Harden the image against the threats you need to mitigate, while still allowing some configuration at runtime so it fits into the wider ecosystem.[1]
When you harden it, ask whether to restrict the execution environment to a specific user.[1]
Also ask whether to limit access to resources.[1]
And ask whether to apply kernel-level restrictions on process execution.[1]
As an example, Iron Bank stores signed container images hardened to the DoD Container Hardening Guide.[3]
Before you deploy the image, check its signature and integrity.[4]
Check its image runtime policies, such as having no malware or critical vulnerabilities.[4]
Check its container runtime policies, such as having no excessive privileges.[4]
Check host vulnerability and compliance controls.[4]
Check workload, application and network security policies.[4]

answer:
GitHub and GitLab let you specify protected branches as well as protected files and folders.[1]
Peribolos, an open source tool that is part of Prow, can declare access control rules for GitHub, and Kubernetes uses it.[1]
gittuf, an OpenSSF sandbox project, is another option, and it also lets you verify that the policy is enforced.[1]
The policy should say which parts of the repository are protected and who can change them, such as a `main` branch that trusted maintainers must approve changes to.[1]

answer:
Test results should be recorded as signed, verifiable attestations and kept in a metadata store, where they can be checked against supply chain policy.[1]
The policy should list every test that is expected, so those tests are confirmed to have run before deployment.[1]
Testing should be considered and attested to at each step of the delivery lifecycle.[1]
During verification, the policy is evaluated against these attestations.[5]
Verifiers look for inconsistencies between what the attestations say happened and what the policy requires.[2]
The signatures on attestations should also be validated, and their contents verified against the software supply chain policy.[3]

answer:
Use The Update Framework (TUF), which uses a "root-of-trust" model to delegate trust from a single root to the teams or developers who sign artifacts.
Set this delegation so that each artifact points to the signing entity you expect for it, such as a build server or a developer.[1]
Clients then use public keys to verify the contents of the repository.[1]
If a validation service signs an artifact after extra checks, delegate to that service's signing key as the trusted key for the artifact.[4]
Make the keys used for each artifact part of a chain of trust that starts from a secure root of trust.[2]
Define user roles in the build pipeline and use them as permission boundaries, so that in high-security environments no single user can attest that a release is valid.[2]

answer:
Delete the pod and create it again with the `--validate` option, for example `kubectl apply --validate -f mypod.yaml`.[1]
If a key name is misspelled, such as `command` written as `commnd`, validation reports an error like `unknown field: commnd`.[1]
Next, export the pod as the apiserver stored it with `kubectl get pods/mypod -o yaml > mypod-on-apiserver.yaml`, and compare that file by hand with your original `mypod.yaml`.[1]
Extra lines in the apiserver version are expected, but lines in your original that are missing from the apiserver version may mean there is a problem with your pod spec.[1]
The usual causes are a section nested in the wrong place or a key name that is typed wrong, and in either case the key is ignored.[1]

The workload resource's controller creates and manages the Pods for you, using the pod template.[2]

answer:
When a container exceeds its memory limit, the kernel kills it with an out-of-memory (OOM) kill.[1]
When a container approaches its CPU limit, it is throttled instead, because the kernel restricts its access to CPU.[1]
In both cases, the kubelet enforces the limits so that the container cannot use more of the resource than its limit.[1]

answer:
Running `kubectl port-forward service/<service-name> forwardedPort:servicePort` against a Service with no selector fails because of a constraint that stops the Kubernetes API server from acting as a proxy.[1]
The constraint keeps callers from using the API server to reach endpoints they may not be authorized to access.[1]
A Service without a selector does not get EndpointSlice objects automatically, so you add them by hand with the network address and port where the backend runs.[2]

answer:
Set up alerts that confirm your Prometheus servers, Alertmanagers, PushGateways and other monitoring infrastructure are up and working correctly.[1]
Where you can, alert on symptoms rather than causes, which cuts down on noise.[1]
For example, one end-to-end blackbox test that checks alerts get from PushGateway to Prometheus to Alertmanager to email is better than a separate alert on each component.[1]
Also add external blackbox monitoring alongside Prometheus's own whitebox monitoring, because it can catch problems you otherwise wouldn't see.[1]
It also gives you a fallback if your internal systems fail completely.[1]

answer:
Query the synthetic `ALERTS` time series, which Prometheus stores for pending and firing alerts, and filter on the `alertname` and `alertstate` labels as needed.[1]

answer:
Duration expressions used with `offset` have to be wrapped in parentheses.[1]
Without the parentheses, the offset calculation uses only the first duration value, so `offset 1h / 2` uses `1h`.[1]
To get a 30 minute offset, write it as `http_requests_total offset (1h / 2)`.[1]

answer:
The `offset` goes inside `sum()`, directly after the selector.[1]
The correct form is `sum(http_requests_total{method="GET"} offset 5m)`.[1]
Putting it outside, as in `sum(http_requests_total{method="GET"}) offset 5m`, is invalid.[1]
